title: Demonstrate an understanding of vine irrigation

lessons.title: How much water vines need
lessons.html:
How much water vines need

Vines need water to grow shoots, leaves and grapes. But for wine grapes, more water is not always better. Too much water makes big, leafy vines and large, watery berries with less flavour. Too little water makes the vine stop growing, leaves turn yellow and fall, and grapes do not ripen properly. The farm manager decides how much water each block gets.

Water needs during the season

StageWater need
Budding and early shoot growth (spring)Moderate; soil is often still moist from winter rain
Flowering and berry setImportant; stress can mean fewer berries
Berry growth (summer)High, especially in hot weather
Ripening (veraison to harvest)Often reduced on purpose for wine grapes, but vines must not be badly stressed
After harvestSome water so leaves stay healthy and store food for next year
WinterUsually little or none; rain is enough in the Western Cape

Young vines

Young vines have small root systems and dry out fast. They need water little and often, and must never be left to wilt.

Signs of water stress

  • Shoot tips stop growing; tendrils hang down or dry up.
  • Leaves droop or turn yellow at the bottom of the shoot.
  • Leaves turn edge-on to the sun in the afternoon.

Signs of too much water

  • Very long, fast-growing shoots and a thick canopy.
  • Water standing on the soil; soft, muddy rows.
  • Yellowing because roots cannot breathe.

Report these signs to your supervisor and write down where you saw them.

lessons.title: Irrigation systems and checks in the vineyard
lessons.html:
Irrigation systems and checks in the vineyard

Systems used in vineyards

  • Drip irrigation: the most common. A pipe runs along each row, often on a low wire, with drippers that give water slowly near each vine. It saves water and keeps leaves dry.
  • Micro-sprinklers: small sprinklers that wet a bigger area of soil. Used in some older or sandy blocks.
  • Dryland: some old bush vines in areas like the Swartland are not irrigated at all.

How the farm decides when to irrigate

The manager uses soil moisture readings (from probes or tensiometers), the weather forecast, the growth stage and the look of the vines. You help by reading the instruments, writing down the numbers and reporting what you see.

Daily irrigation checks

  1. Check filters at the pump station and clean them if dirty.
  2. Check the pressure gauge; write down the reading.
  3. Walk the rows. Look for leaks, burst pipes, pipes chewed by animals and drippers that are blocked or missing.
  4. Check that the pipe is in place and drippers are near the vines, not dripping onto the trunk or away in the middle of the row.
  5. Check the end of the line for low flow.
  6. Flush the lines as the farm schedule says, to remove dirt.
  7. Record the block, hours run and water meter readings.

Fertigation

Some farms add fertiliser into the irrigation water. This is called fertigation. Only trained workers may mix and inject fertiliser, with the right PPE. Never drink water from the drip lines.

Saving water

Water is scarce in South Africa and its use is controlled by the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Fixing leaks fast, irrigating at the right time and not over-watering all save water and money.

Safety

  • Leave pump and electrical work to qualified people.
  • Keep hands away from moving pump parts.

Key points

  • Vines need the right amount of water at each stage: not too much and not too little.
  • Young vines must never be allowed to wilt.
  • Know the signs of water stress and over-watering.
  • Drip irrigation is common; check filters, pressure, leaks and drippers daily.
  • Record readings and report problems; never drink water from drip lines.
